touches.text: Trouble Ticket: an error that needs a non-automated fixer (CC or Akien).

A trouble ticket is a work order. Whoever fixed it reports the fix to the originator (the device or machine that raised it), and the originator marks it fixed. A trouble that comes back is not designed for yet; if recurrent problems appear, we'll explore that.
Trouble: it has to be able to report when nothing else can, so a direct line makes sense for recovery (6.3.4).
Cairn's own sleep has a lot to do, including clearing the logging tree of things older than 30 days (4.3.2).
Trouble tickets (3.4.3) live here. Any device has a direct line to raise one, not over the bus (2.3.7.1.3).
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).

VERBS: activate, charter, deposit, drain, feedback, question, sealed (plus get and show). Moving a ticket across its workflow is the ticket's own act; CodeMother's gates only answer it (3.3.4). Each chart stage (orient through validate) and the verdict is a gate machine that answers queueme <fileref>; the ticket class queues itself to each in turn (3.3.4.3), so there is no chart or verdict verb, and `cross` leaves with the harbor's `clear` (9.4.1.5).

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
